newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Clinton, Starr clash on Whitewater probe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Starr clash on Whitewater probe.

text.p: President Clinton and Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr clashed publicly Saturday on whether the White House is using legalities to stall Starr's inquiry.

Starr, in a speech in Heber Springs, Ark., commented on Clinton's decision to appeal to the Supreme Court a ruling ordering the release of notes taken by White House lawyers during conversations with first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis, deciding in Starr's favour, ruled last month that attorney-client privilege did not apply to the notes, which related to the long investigation into the Arkansas Whitewater financial affair.

But the White House announced May 2 it would appeal the decision to the Supreme Court. The Clintons, who have publicly touted their cooperation with Starr's investigation, have long denied any wrongdoing in the complex web of Arkansas business deals, political contacts and allegations of cover-up known as Whitewater.

Starr, after discussing legal hindrances in other cases, said of his Whitewater inquiry: "We faced a different sort of impediment in another grand jury matter ... We sought to learn what Mrs. Clinton had related, in two separate meetings, to attorneys from the White House counsel's office."
He added: "The White House refused to turn over the subpoenaed notes, insisting that the meetings were shielded by a governmental attorney-client privilege."

Clinton, asked at a news conference with Caribbean leaders whether he felt there was personal animosity between him and Starr, said: "Not on my part ... I'm just over here doing my job in the Caribbean."

He said White House counsel Charles Ruff had strongly recommended that the lower court ruling be appealed to protect the attorney-client privilege -- the right of clients to have confidential conversations with their lawyers.

Clinton said Ruff "came to me and said that the effect of the decision would be not confined to the president, the first lady and the chief of staff at the White House, that the position that the special counsel was arguing for would in effect abolish the lawyer-client privilege between a federal government lawyer and a federal employee at any level under any circumstance."
He added: "Now the law firms in America might be ecstatic about that because it would certainly make a lot more private business for lawyers."
Clinton said Ruff told him, "I cannot tell you how emphatically I believe that this case must be appealed" because it represented a "major constitutional question."

Clinton's reaction was relatively low-key compared to his tart response Tuesday in Mexico City to questions about a court document indicating that Starr believed there were discrepancies in the first lady's testimony.
Starr said he was commenting publicly on the case because the White House had talked about it.
Although the appeals court agreed with Starr's position, he now must wait for the Supreme Court to decide if it will hear the case, perhaps by the end of next month.
"Disputes about the law, like the one that led to the Eighth Circuit ruling, invariably slow down an investigation," Starr said.

One set of the notes in question was based on what Mrs. Clinton told White House lawyers about her grand jury testimony on Jan. 26, 1996, when she testified she did not know how a set of Whitewater-related legal billing records ended up in a library in the White House residence.

Another set of notes dated from July 11, 1995, and concerned Mrs. Clinton's activities in the days following the July 1993 suicide of deputy White House legal counsel Vince Foster, who worked with Mrs. Clinton at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock, Ark., when President Clinton was governor of that state.
